title: Angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2)
hook: welcome strangers; some have hosted angels without knowing

segments.voice: Yesterday: alms, gifts to the poor, given without a trumpet. Your line was let it stay secret. Did you manage one quiet gift, and not tell anyone? Day one hundred thirty-four.

It's the hottest part of the day. An old man is sitting in the doorway of his tent, the kind of heat where nobody moves. He looks up and there are three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait for them to ask. He runs. An old man, running in that heat. He bows, begs them to stay, fetches water to wash their feet, tells his wife to bake bread from the good flour, picks out a calf himself. He calls it a little bread. It's a feast. He stands under a tree while they eat. The man is Abraham, in Genesis chapter eighteen, and before the day is over he learns who his guests really were. Much later, a letter in the New Testament seems to remember that afternoon. Today's word is what Abraham did.
screen: `THE HOTTEST PART OF THE DAY.` → `THREE STRANGERS.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS.`

segments.voice: Hospitality. In the New Testament the Greek word is philoxenia. Philo, love. Xenos, stranger. Love of the stranger. Not love of your friends, which is easy, but of the person you don't know yet. The letter to the Hebrews, near its end, gives a short list of how to live, and this is on it. In the King James Bible: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares. Without knowing. Readers have long heard Abraham in that line, though the letter never names him: the visitors at his tent turn out to be messengers of God, and in the story one of them promises that old Sarah will have a son. Abraham didn't welcome them because they were angels. He welcomed them, and they turned out to be. That's the order. In the world of these stories, this was not a small courtesy. A traveler far from home depended on someone's open door for food and safety. Opening your door could be a lifeline, and it could cost you. Christians carried the practice forward. Jesus says in Matthew that at the end, the king will say: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Saint Benedict, writing a rule for monks, said every guest should be welcomed as Christ, and he quoted that same line from Matthew. Jewish tradition treasures the same story: welcoming guests is counted a mitzvah, a commandment, and Abraham's open tent is its picture. So the idea is simple, and harder than it sounds: the person at your door might carry more than you can see.
screen: `PHILOXENIA — LOVE OF THE STRANGER.` · `SOME HAVE ENTERTAINED ANGELS.` · `AN OPEN DOOR, A LIFELINE.` · `EVERY GUEST AS CHRIST.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Picture your own door: your apartment, your desk at work, your spot in the cafeteria. Who comes to it that you barely notice? The delivery driver. The new person on the team. The neighbor you've nodded at for two years. Pick one face. Now imagine offering them something small to drink: water, a coffee, a cold soda on a hot day. Just that. If you pray, you can ask to see that person clearly. If you don't, simply hold their face for a moment with a little more warmth than usual. The bell holds the time.
Hospitality. In Greek, philoxenia, love of the stranger. Abraham ran to his guests before he knew who they were.
Your line: strangers might be angels. Today, offer one guest or visitor something to drink, and see who they turn out to be. Day one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Many Christians practice hospitality by welcoming visitors at church, opening their homes for meals, and hosting travelers; some monasteries keep guesthouses for visitors, following Saint Benedict's rule to receive guests as Christ.

original.note: Greek: love of the stranger — philo, love, and xenos, stranger.

trapdoor: what you thought: hospitality means being a good host at dinner parties.
what it means: welcoming the stranger, the one you don't know yet, as if they might carry more than you can see.
what a scholar hears: philoxenia. xenos means both stranger and guest, and for a traveler far from home, an open door meant food and safety.

notes: Genesis 18: the visitors are called three men, and the LORD appears to Abraham; interpretations differ on whether all three are angels or one is the LORD. Script says 'messengers of God'. Confirm this is acceptable.
Hebrews 13:2 as an allusion to Abraham (and Lot, Genesis 19): standard reading. Confirm.
Rule of Benedict ch. 53 (c. 530s): 'All guests who present themselves are to be welcomed as Christ' — paraphrased only. 'Around fifteen hundred years ago' — confirm.
Hachnasat orchim (welcoming guests) as a Jewish commandment/mitzvah, with Abraham as its model: confirm phrasing.
Myth item on ancient travel safety: general claim; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the trapdoor said the ancient world had no inns (Luke 2:7 has one): fixed. Cut 'most readers', 'around fifteen hundred years ago', 'many monasteries still keep a guesthouse because of that line', 'many Jewish families' and the general no-hotels claim. Benedict is now said to quote Matthew 25:35 (Rule ch. 53.1; confirm). The myth about ancient travel safety is replaced with one taught today: Hebrews 13:2 never names Abraham.
